text: The sky appears blue because of a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Sunlight contains all colors of the visible spectrum, and when it enters Earth's atmosphere, it collides with tiny gas molecules (mostly nitrogen and oxygen). These molecules scatter shorter wavelengths of light—like blue and violet—much more strongly than longer wavelengths like red and orange. In fact, blue light is scattered roughly four times more than red light. This scattered blue light bounces around the atmosphere in all directions, so no matter where you look in the sky, blue light reaches your eyes. Violet is actually scattered even more than blue, but the sky doesn't look purple because the sun emits less violet light, some of it is absorbed by the upper atmosphere, and our eyes are more sensitive to blue. This same effect explains why sunsets appear red and orange: when the sun is low on the horizon, its light travels through more atmosphere, and by the time it reaches you, most of the blue light has been scattered away, leaving the warmer colors behind.
